plan.chapterName: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 15.2.12
plan.contextChunk: This figure is part of a worked example that evaluates the line integral of F = cos(x) i + sin(x) j along two different oriented curves. The figure contains two panels (a) and (b), each showing the same vector field F drawn over a green-shaded background with the note Vectors not to scale. Panel (a): the oriented curve C is a short vertical red line segment at x = -pi/2, directed downards from y = 2 to y = 1. Panel (b): the oriented curve C is a parabolic arc from (-1, 1) to (2, 4), directed first down, then upward and to the right. The figure shows the two distinct integration paths for parts (a) and (b) of the example, making visible how each curve's geometry and alignment relative to the field vectors determines the computed line integral. Note that the two parts of the image are differently scaled.

interactionPlan.concept: The line integral of a vector field along a curve accumulates the component of the field tangent to the path, so the value depends on both the path's geometry and its alignment with the field — and because F = cos(x)i + sin(x)j is not conservative, reshaping the path changes the result.
elements: x-axis and y-axis with arrowheads and italic labels x, y
light-green shaded rectangular background region behind the field
grid of short black vector-field arrows representing F = cos(x)i + sin(x)j (not to scale)
annotation 'Vectors not to scale' above the field
panel (a) tick labels: x at -pi/2, y at 1 and 2
panel (a) oriented curve C: red vertical segment at x = -pi/2 from y = 2 down to y = 1, with red endpoint dots, a red arrowhead pointing downward, and label C
panel (b) tick labels: x at -2,-1,1,2,3 and y at 1,2,3,4
panel (b) oriented curve C: red parabolic arc from (-1,1) through (0,0) to (2,4), with red endpoint dots, red arrowheads showing direction (down then up-right), and label C
moving point marker (filled dot) traveling along C
field vector F drawn at the moving point (dark arrow)
unit tangent vector T drawn at the moving point (red arrow)
numeric readout of the local integrand F·T and the running accumulated line integral value

interactions.label: Integration path
interactions.teaches: The same field integrated over two different curves gives different values because each path samples different field vectors over a different length and alignment

interactions.label: Position t along C
interactions.teaches: Sweeping t moves a point along C and reveals the integrand F·T at each location — the line integral is exactly the accumulation of these tangential components
Because F is not conservative (curl F != 0), dragging the endpoints to reshape C changes the computed line integral, demonstrating path-dependence

demo_steps.title: Vertical path (a)
demo_steps.narration: On the short vertical segment at x = -pi/2 the field is nearly vertical, so the tangent aligns with F and the integrand F·T is large and negative (path goes downward).

demo_steps.title: Sweep the integrand
demo_steps.narration: Drag the t slider to move the point down the segment; watch the field vector, the tangent vector, and the F·T readout, and see the accumulated integral build up.

demo_steps.title: Curved path (b)
demo_steps.narration: Toggle to the parabolic arc: the tangent direction now varies continuously, so F·T changes sign along the path and the total integral differs from part (a).

demo_steps.title: Reshape and compare
demo_steps.narration: Drag an endpoint of C to deform the path through the same field; the line integral value updates in real time, confirming the result depends on the chosen path.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A line integral sums the tangential component F·T along the curve, so the answer is set by how the path threads through the field — and for a non-conservative field like this one, changing the path changes the value.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Render one panel at a time per the toggle. Light-green background rectangle; a regular grid of short black arrows for F = cos(x)i + sin(x)j (arrows point down-left for x<-pi/2 region, rotate to rightward near x=0, then up-right for x>0 in panel a; in panel b they form the saddle-like pattern seen in the figure). Curve C in bold red with red endpoint dots and red direction arrowheads, labeled C in italic. The moving point is a solid dot; draw the field vector at it as a dark arrow and the unit tangent as a red arrow, with a small text readout 'F·T = ...' and '∫_C F·dr = ...' updating live. Keep the 'Vectors not to scale' note at top. Panel (a) x-tick at -pi/2 and y-ticks 1,2; panel (b) x-ticks -2..3 and y-ticks 1..4. Use distinct red vs dark coloring so the tangent and field vectors at the moving point are never confused.

- Toggle between the two panels (short vertical path vs. long curved path) to compare how path shape and length affect the line integral value over the same field
- Slider for parameter t: animate a moving point along C and display the field vector and its dot product with the tangent at each step

discrepancies: Vector field arrow density is noticeably lower than the source (~9×9 grid vs ~12×12 in the original), making the field look sparser
The red path C in panel (a) shows multiple small arrowheads along the segment instead of the single triangular arrowhead at the midpoint used in the source
A legend (F/T arrows) and live numeric readout (F·T, integral values) are added in the top-left corner, not present in the source figure
The black field-vector arrow drawn at the current slider position extends below the bottom endpoint dot, adding visual clutter not in the static source
evaluation.notes: The figure faithfully reproduces both panels of the source (correct vector field F=cos(x)i+sin(x)j, correct path geometries, correct axis ranges and tick labels) and adds excellent pedagogically-meaningful interactions (panel toggle, position slider, draggable endpoints, guided demo steps with live integral readout); the main visual gaps are lower arrow density and minor stylistic differences in path arrowheads.
action_items: Increase vector field arrow density by reducing stepX to ~0.38 and stepY to ~0.35 to better match the source's ~12×12 grid
Replace the multiple small arrowheads on path C with a single larger triangular arrowhead at the midpoint, matching the source's style
Consider hiding or reducing the opacity of the black F-vector arrow at t=0 so it doesn't visually collide with the bottom endpoint dot
